title: Yo-Irregulars and Ir a
bigQuestion: Why do some of the most common Spanish verbs break the pattern, and how do you talk about plans?

story.title: Packing for Guadalajara
story.kicker: A family trip to see relatives means plans, packing and a lot of irregular verbs.
paragraphs: Daniel is sixteen and lives in Little Village with his mom and his younger sister, Ana. In two weeks, they are flying to Guadalajara, in the Mexican state of Jalisco, to visit his grandmother. Daniel's mom calls it the trip of the year. Daniel calls it the week without his friends, but secretly he is excited.

At dinner his mom makes a list. "Yo hago las maletas el viernes" (I pack the suitcases on Friday), she says. "Tú traes los regalos para la familia" (You bring the gifts for the family). Daniel answers, "Yo traigo los regalos, pero no sé qué comprar" (I'll bring the gifts, but I don't know what to buy).

Ana has a question. "¿Conoces a los primos de Zapopan?" (Do you know the cousins from Zapopan?). Daniel shakes his head. "No los conozco. Sé sus nombres, nada más" (I don't know them. I know their names, nothing more). He has seen them only in photos on his grandmother's phone.

Then his mom reads the plan for the week out loud. "El sábado vamos a visitar a la abuela. El domingo vamos a ir al centro. El lunes, ustedes van a conocer a los primos" (On Saturday we're going to visit Grandma. On Sunday we're going to go downtown. On Monday, you two are going to meet the cousins).

That night Daniel texts his best friend, Kevin. "Salgo el día quince. Voy a Guadalajara. Vengo el veintidós" (I leave on the fifteenth. I'm going to Guadalajara. I come back on the twenty-second). Kevin writes back, "¿Qué vas a hacer allá?" (What are you going to do there?). Daniel smiles and types, "Voy a comer mucho."
story.think: Daniel uses sé for knowing names but conozco for knowing people. What do you think is the difference?

lessons.title: Verbs with -go in the Yo Form
lessons.mainIdea: Some common verbs add a g in the yo form, like hago, pongo, salgo and traigo, but stay regular elsewhere.
reading: Daniel's mom says, "Yo *hago* las maletas" (I pack the suitcases, literally I make the suitcases). If hacer (to do, to make) were regular, the yo form would be "haco." But it is hago. Hacer belongs to a small group called the yo-go verbs, because the yo form ends in -go.

Four of the most useful yo-go verbs are hacer, *poner* (to put), *salir* (to leave, go out) and *traer* (to bring). Their yo forms are hago, pongo, salgo and traigo. Here is the good news: in the other forms, they are regular. Hacer goes hago, haces, hace, hacemos, hacéis, hacen. Salir goes salgo, sales, sale, salimos, salís, salen.

A common mistake is to keep the g in every form: "tú hagas" or "ella pongue." Only yo gets the g. Another mistake is to make yo regular: "yo salo" or "yo trao." Those forms sound natural to a learner, but no native speaker says them. Memorize the yo form and use regular endings everywhere else.

words.d: to do or make — yo hago, tú haces, él hace; hacer la maleta = to pack a suitcase
to put or place — yo pongo, tú pones, él pone
to leave or go out — yo salgo, tú sales, él sale, nosotros salimos
to bring — yo traigo, tú traes, él trae

look.title: Packing Night
look.text: Mamá: ¿Qué haces? Daniel: Hago mi maleta. Pongo la ropa aquí y traigo los zapatos. Mamá: ¿Y cuándo sales? Daniel: Salgo el viernes con ustedes, mamá. ¡Tú sabes!
look.prompt: Find the four yo-go forms in Daniel's lines. Then say which forms in the dialogue are regular.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Yo ___ la mesa antes de comer. (poner)
check.why: Poner is a yo-go verb: yo pongo.

check.q: Choose the correct form: ¿A qué hora ___ tú de la escuela? (salir)
check.why: Only yo gets the g. Tú takes the regular -ir ending: sales.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Traer has the irregular yo form traigo.

lessons.title: Tener, Venir and Decir
lessons.mainIdea: Tener, venir and decir have -go in the yo form and also change their stem in other forms.
reading: Ana asks her brother, "¿Tienes el pasaporte?" (Do you have the passport?). Daniel checks his backpack. "Sí, *tengo* el pasaporte" (Yes, I have the passport). Tener (to have) is a yo-go verb, but it has an extra twist. In some forms, the e in the stem becomes ie: tienes, tiene, tienen.

Here is tener in full: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen. *Venir* (to come) follows the same shape: vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, venís, vienen. Notice that nosotros and vosotros keep the plain stem. You will learn more about this stem change, called the boot pattern, in the next unit.

*Decir* (to say, to tell) is similar but changes e to i: digo, dices, dice, decimos, decís, dicen. English speakers often say "yo teno" or "tú tenes" because they expect a regular pattern. Practice these three verbs out loud until tengo, vengo and digo sound automatic, because you will use them every day.

words.d: to have — tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen
to come — vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, venís, vienen
to say or tell — digo, dices, dice, decimos, decís, dicen

look.title: Three Verbs, Side by Side
look.text: yo: tengo / vengo / digo. tú: tienes / vienes / dices. él: tiene / viene / dice. nosotros: tenemos / venimos / decimos. vosotros: tenéis / venís / decís. ellos: tienen / vienen / dicen.
look.prompt: Which two forms of each verb keep the same stem vowel as the infinitive?

check.q: Choose the correct form: Mi abuela ___ tres gatos. (tener)
check.why: Tener changes e to ie for ella: tiene.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Nosotros ___ de Chicago. (venir)
check.why: Nosotros keeps the plain stem: venimos.

check.q: How do you say "I always tell the truth"?
check.why: Decir has the irregular yo form digo.

lessons.title: Conozco, Doy and Veo
lessons.mainIdea: A few other verbs are irregular only in the yo form: conozco, sé, doy and veo.
reading: Daniel says, "No *conozco* a los primos" (I don't know the cousins). Conocer (to know, to be familiar with) is regular in every form except yo, where it adds a z: conozco. Many verbs ending in -cer or -cir after a vowel do the same, like parecer (parezco) and traducir (traduzco).

*Dar* (to give) has the yo form doy, and the rest is simple: das, da, damos, dais, dan. Notice that dais has no accent because it is only one syllable. *Ver* (to see) has the yo form veo, and then ves, ve, vemos, veis, ven. These verbs are short, so the irregular yo form stands out.

Saber (to know a fact) has the most surprising yo form of all: sé. It has an accent mark to tell it apart from se, a different little word. The rest of saber is regular: sabes, sabe, sabemos, sabéis, saben. Learners often write "yo sabo," which follows the pattern but is wrong. Say "No sé" (I don't know) every time you want to practice.

words.d: to know or be familiar with a person or place — yo conozco, tú conoces
to give — yo doy, tú das, él da, nosotros damos
to see or watch — yo veo, tú ves, él ve, nosotros vemos
to know a fact or how to do something — yo sé, tú sabes, él sabe

look.title: At the Airport Gate
look.text: Ana: ¿Ves a mamá? Daniel: No, no la veo. Ana: ¿Sabes la puerta? Daniel: Sí, sé la puerta: la B12. Doy los boletos a la señora y vamos.
look.prompt: Find the three irregular yo forms in Daniel's lines.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Yo ___ la respuesta. (saber)
check.why: Saber has the irregular yo form sé, with an accent mark.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Yo ___ un regalo a mi abuela. (dar)
check.why: Dar has the irregular yo form doy.

check.q: Which form is correct for "you see" (tú)?
check.why: Only the yo form of ver is irregular. Tú is ves.

lessons.title: Knowing Facts: Saber
lessons.mainIdea: Use saber for facts, information and knowing how to do something.
reading: Kevin asks Daniel, "¿Sabes cuándo sales?" (Do you know when you leave?). Daniel answers, "Sí, sé la fecha: el quince" (Yes, I know the date: the fifteenth). A date is a fact, a piece of information. When you know information, Spanish uses *saber*. English uses one verb, know, for many things. Spanish splits it into two.

Saber is also used before an infinitive to mean "to know how to." "Sé nadar" means "I know how to swim." "Mi abuela sabe cocinar birria" means "My grandmother knows how to cook birria." Notice that Spanish does not need a word for "how" in this meaning. English speakers often add cómo, but "sé cómo nadar" is not the usual way to say it.

Saber often comes before question words or si (whether, if). "No sé dónde está el pasaporte" (I don't know where the passport is). "¿Sabes si llueve en Guadalajara?" (Do you know if it rains in Guadalajara?). If the thing you know could be written down as an *información* (piece of information), saber is usually the right choice.

words.d: to know a fact, or to know how to do something — sé, sabes, sabe
information — something you can know with saber
to swim — a regular -ar verb; Sé nadar. (I know how to swim.)

look.title: Facts Daniel Knows
look.text: Daniel sabe la dirección de su abuela. Sabe que el vuelo sale a las seis. Sabe hablar español e inglés. Pero no sabe bailar. (But he doesn't know how to dance.)
look.prompt: Say two things you know how to do using sé + an infinitive.

check.q: Choose the correct verb: ¿___ tú a qué hora sale el vuelo?
check.why: The time of a flight is a fact, so saber is right, and tú takes sabes.

check.q: How do you say "She knows how to cook"?
check.why: Saber plus an infinitive means to know how to; ella takes sabe.

check.q: Which sentence needs saber?
choices: I know where the hotel is.
I know that song's singer personally.
check.why: Knowing where something is means knowing information, so it uses saber.

lessons.title: Knowing People and Places: Conocer
lessons.mainIdea: Use conocer for being familiar with people, places and things, and add a before a person.
reading: Ana asks, "¿*Conoces* a los primos?" (Do you know the cousins?). You cannot write a person down as a fact, so this is conocer. Conocer means to know in the sense of being acquainted or familiar. You conocer a person, a city, a restaurant or a song. "Conozco Chicago muy bien" (I know Chicago very well).

When the thing you know is a person, Spanish adds a small word, a, before the person. This is called the *a personal*. "Conozco a tu mamá" (I know your mom). "No conocemos a los primos" (We don't know the cousins). There is no English word for it, so English speakers often leave it out. With places, you do not use it: "Conozco Guadalajara."

Conocer can also mean to meet someone for the first time. "El lunes vamos a conocer a los primos" means "On Monday we are going to meet the cousins." So a quick test helps: if you mean acquainted with or meet, use conocer. If you mean information or how to do something, use saber.

words.d: to know a person, place or thing; to meet for the first time — conozco, conoces, conoce
the personal a — a small word placed before a person who receives the action: Conozco a Ana.
the cousin (male / female); los primos = the cousins

look.title: Saber or Conocer?
look.text: Sé tu número de teléfono. (a fact) Conozco a tu hermano. (a person) Conozco la Plaza Tapatía. (a place) Sé que la plaza está en el centro. (a fact) Sé tocar la guitarra. (how to) Quiero conocer a tu abuela. (to meet)
look.prompt: Make one sentence with sé and one with conozco about your own neighborhood.

check.q: Choose the correct sentence.
check.why: Knowing a person uses conocer, and the personal a comes before the person.

check.q: Choose the correct verb: Nosotros no ___ Guadalajara todavía.
check.why: Being familiar with a place uses conocer; nosotros takes conocemos.

check.q: What does "Vamos a conocer a los primos" mean?
choices: We are going to meet the cousins.
We are going to call the cousins.
check.why: Conocer a someone for the first time means to meet them.

lessons.title: Choosing Between Them
lessons.mainIdea: Ask yourself: is it a fact or skill (saber), or a person, place or first meeting (conocer)?
reading: Daniel's grandmother calls on video. "¿Sabes mi dirección?" (Do you know my address?). "Sí, abuela, la sé" (Yes, Grandma, I know it). "¿Y conoces mi barrio?" (And do you know my neighborhood?). "No, no lo conozco" (No, I don't know it). One conversation, both verbs, and each has its own job.

Here is a quick *prueba* (test) you can run in your head. Can you finish the sentence with a fact, a question word or an infinitive? Then use saber: sé que, sé dónde, sé nadar. Is the thing a person, a place or something you have experienced, like a book or a song? Then use conocer: conozco a Ana, conozco Pilsen, conozco esa canción.

Heritage speakers usually choose correctly by ear, but it helps to name the rule when writing. New learners often choose saber for everything because it feels closer to "know." A good habit is to picture the object. If you can shake hands with it or walk around in it, you probably need *conocer*.

words.d: the test or quiz — here, a quick check for choosing saber or conocer
the neighborhood — Conozco el barrio. (I know the neighborhood.)
the address — Sé la dirección. (I know the address.)

look.title: Sort Them Out
look.text: 1. ___ la respuesta. 2. ___ a la profesora nueva. 3. ___ tocar el piano. 4. ___ el Museo Nacional de Arte Mexicano en Pilsen. 5. ___ dónde vive Kevin. Answers: sé, conozco, sé, conozco, sé.
look.prompt: For each answer, say which clue told you: a fact, a person, a skill or a place.

check.q: Choose the correct verb: Yo no ___ dónde está mi teléfono.
check.why: Dónde introduces information, so use saber: no sé.

check.q: Choose the correct verb: ¿Ustedes ___ el barrio de Pilsen?
check.why: Being familiar with a place uses conocer; ustedes takes conocen.

check.q: Which pair is correct?
check.why: Saber + infinitive for a skill; conocer + a for a person.

lessons.title: The Verb Ir
lessons.mainIdea: Ir (to go) is fully irregular: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van.
reading: Daniel tells his friend, "*Voy* a Guadalajara" (I'm going to Guadalajara). Voy comes from the infinitive *ir* (to go). Ir is so irregular that none of its present forms look like the infinitive. You cannot find a stem to drop. You just memorize it: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van.

The good news is that once you learn voy, the rest follows an -ar pattern with the letter v: v-as, v-a, v-amos, v-ais, v-an. The vosotros form, vais, has no accent because it is one syllable. Ir is almost always followed by a (to) and a place. When a meets el, they join into al: "Vamos al centro" (We're going downtown).

Learners sometimes say "yo vo" or "nosotros imos," trying to build forms from ir. Others forget the contraction and say "a el parque." Spanish always writes al for a + el. But a + la stays two words: "Voy a la playa" (I'm going to the beach). Only el combines.

words.d: to go — voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van
to the — the required joining of a + el: Voy al mercado.
downtown, the center of a city — Vamos al centro.

look.title: Ir: Six Forms, One Pattern
look.prompt: Which form of ir is the only one with two syllables?

check.q: Choose the correct form: Nosotros ___ al mercado. (ir)
check.why: Ir is irregular; nosotros is vamos. Vemos comes from ver.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Ella takes va, and a + el must join as al.

check.q: Choose the correct form: ¿Adónde ___ tú el sábado? (ir)
check.why: Tú takes vas.

lessons.title: Ir a + Infinitive
lessons.mainIdea: To talk about the near future, use a form of ir, then a, then an infinitive: Voy a comer.
reading: Kevin texts, "¿Qué vas a hacer allá?" (What are you going to do there?). Daniel answers, "Voy a comer mucho" (I'm going to eat a lot). This pattern is called ir a + *infinitive*. It works just like "going to" in English, which makes it one of the easiest ways to talk about the *futuro* (future).

The formula has three parts. First, conjugate ir for the subject: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van. Second, add a. Third, add the verb in its infinitive form, with no changes. "Ana va a visitar a la abuela." "Nosotros vamos a salir el viernes." "Ustedes van a conocer a los primos." Only ir changes; the second verb never does.

The two most common mistakes are forgetting a and conjugating the second verb. "Voy comer" is missing a. "Voy a como" conjugates the second verb, which is wrong. Check both parts each time. You can also add time words to show when: mañana (tomorrow), el fin de semana (the weekend), esta noche (tonight).

words.d: going to + verb — the near future: Voy a estudiar. (I'm going to study.)
the future — time that has not happened yet
tomorrow — Mañana voy a trabajar. (La mañana, with la, means the morning.)

look.title: Mom's Plan for the Week
look.text: El sábado vamos a visitar a la abuela. El domingo vamos a ir al centro. El lunes ustedes van a conocer a los primos. El martes yo voy a descansar. (On Tuesday I'm going to rest.)
look.prompt: Write one line about what you are going to do this weekend, using voy a + an infinitive.

check.q: Which sentence correctly says "We are going to travel"?
check.why: Conjugate ir for nosotros (vamos), then a, then the infinitive viajar.

check.q: What does "Mis primos van a venir mañana" mean?
choices: My cousins are going to come tomorrow.
My cousins are going to go tomorrow morning.
check.why: Van a venir is ir a + infinitive for the near future, and mañana means tomorrow.

check.q: What is wrong with "Voy a como tacos"?
choices: the second verb should be the infinitive comer
check.why: In ir a + infinitive, only ir is conjugated; the second verb stays as comer.

lessons.title: Planning a Weekend
lessons.mainIdea: Combine ir a, days of the week and yo-irregulars to describe weekend plans clearly.
reading: Before the trip, Daniel's friends plan a weekend in Chicago. Kevin says, "El sábado voy a jugar fútbol en el parque. ¿Vienes?" (On Saturday I'm going to play soccer in the park. Are you coming?). Daniel says, "No puedo. *Tengo que* hacer la maleta" (I can't. I have to pack). Tener que plus an infinitive means "to have to."

Plans often mix the present and ir a. The present can describe a fixed schedule: "El vuelo sale el viernes" (The flight leaves on Friday). Ir a describes what you intend: "Voy a dormir en el avión" (I'm going to sleep on the plane). Both are correct, and native speakers use them side by side in the same conversation.

Days of the week in Spanish are not capitalized: lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo. Use el for one day (el sábado, this Saturday) and los for a habit (los sábados, on Saturdays). Put it all together and you can say a lot: "El *fin de semana* salgo con mi familia y vamos a comer en casa de mi tía."

words.d: to have to do something — Tengo que estudiar. (I have to study.)
the weekend — Este fin de semana voy a descansar.
Saturday, or this Saturday — los sábados means on Saturdays, every week

look.title: Two Friends, Two Plans
look.text: Kevin: ¿Qué vas a hacer el domingo? Daniel: Voy a ver a mi tía. Ella hace tamales. ¿Y tú? Kevin: Tengo que trabajar, pero después salgo con mi hermano. Vamos a ir al cine.
look.prompt: List every verb in the dialogue and say whether it is a regular present, an irregular present or ir a + infinitive.

check.q: How do you say "I have to leave early"?
check.why: Tener que + infinitive: tengo que salir.

check.q: What does "Los domingos comemos con mi abuela" mean?
choices: This Sunday we are going to eat with my grandmother.
Last Sunday we ate with my grandmother.
On Sundays my grandmother eats alone.
On Sundays we eat with my grandmother.
check.why: Los domingos shows a weekly habit, and comemos is the present for nosotros.

check.q: Choose the correct plan: El viernes, yo ___ con mis amigos. (salir)
check.why: Salir is a yo-go verb: yo salgo.

lessons.title: Talking About a Trip
lessons.mainIdea: A short trip description uses ir, ir a, the yo-go verbs and saber or conocer together.
reading: On the plane, Daniel writes a short message to post when he lands. "Hoy voy a Guadalajara. Traigo regalos para mi abuela. No conozco a mis primos, pero voy a conocerlos mañana. No sé qué vamos a hacer, pero sé que vamos a comer bien." Every verb from this chapter is in those few lines.

Guadalajara is the capital of the state of Jalisco and one of the largest cities in Mexico. Jalisco is widely known as the home of mariachi music and of tequila, which is named after a town in the state. People from Guadalajara are often called *tapatíos* (people from Guadalajara). Many families in Chicago have roots in Jalisco and visit relatives there.

When you describe a trip, start with where you are going (voy a…), then what you bring or do (traigo, hago), then who or what you know (conozco, sé), and finish with plans (voy a + infinitive). This simple order helps you write a clear paragraph. It also lets you check each verb against the rule you learned for it.

words.d: the trip — Hago un viaje a Guadalajara. (I'm taking a trip to Guadalajara.)
a person from Guadalajara, or something from Guadalajara
the gift — Traigo un regalo para mi abuela.

look.title: Daniel's Post, Verb by Verb
look.text: voy → ir, irregular. traigo → traer, yo-go. conozco → conocer, yo form with z. voy a conocerlos → ir a + infinitive, with the pronoun los attached. sé → saber, irregular yo. vamos a comer → ir a + infinitive.
look.prompt: Write a four-sentence post about a trip you would like to take, using at least three verbs from this chapter.

check.q: What does "No sé qué vamos a hacer" mean?
choices: I don't know what we did.
I don't know what we are going to do.
We don't know how to do it.
check.why: No sé means I don't know, and vamos a hacer is the near future for nosotros.

check.q: What is a tapatío?
choices: a type of taco from Chicago
check.why: Tapatío is the common name for someone or something from Guadalajara.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Mañana yo ___ a conocer a mis primos. (ir)
check.why: Yo takes voy in ir a + infinitive.

review.q: Choose the correct form: Yo ___ la tarea después de cenar. (hacer)
review.why: Hacer is a yo-go verb: yo hago.

review.q: Choose the correct form: Ellos ___ de México. (venir)
review.why: Venir changes e to ie for ellos: vienen.
Knowing a person uses conocer plus the personal a.
Saber + infinitive means to know how to; yo is sé.

review.q: How do you say "They are going to visit us"?
review.why: Ellos takes van, then a, then the infinitive visitar with nos attached.

review.q: Which sentence uses the contraction correctly?
review.why: A + el must join as al; centro is masculine.

review.q: Choose the correct form: Yo ___ el libro en la mesa. (poner)
review.why: Poner is a yo-go verb: yo pongo.

review.q: What does "¿Qué vas a traer?" mean?
choices: Who is going to bring it?
What are you going to bring?
review.why: Vas a traer is ir a + infinitive for tú: you are going to bring.
